en: Two qubits on a lab bench. Is that even a computer?
A qubit is a quantum bit, the unit a quantum computer works with.
For seventeen years, quantum computers stayed about that small: 2 qubits in 1998, 12 at most.
In the next nine years, one chip held over a thousand. What changed?
Meet two people we made up: an old physicist, and a young computer-science student.
In 1998, machines like his had two qubits: molecules in a liquid, read by magnets.
They ran tiny demos, like finding one item out of four in a single look.
It works. So, back to the question: is it a computer? A gate is one basic step of a quantum program.
This chart is from the first lecture of Professor Yufei Ding's course on quantum computing systems, at UC San Diego.
Look at its title.
The first stretch is the past seventeen years, 1998 to 2015.
The slide says 7 to 12: those are the biggest ones, 7 qubits in 2000, then 12 in 2006. So the red pen writes 2 to 12.
And under the numbers, two words: lab access.
For our student, that meant a locked door. The machine lived in one lab.
So a computer-science student could only stand on tiptoe and look through the glass.
Then, from 2016 on, the door began to give.
In May 2016, IBM put a five-qubit quantum computer online for anyone to try.
The door was still shut, but now it had a mail slot.
That is cloud access: the machine stays in the builder's lab, and you send it a program from your laptop over the internet. Programs in, answers out.
Meanwhile, the chips kept growing.
127 qubits in 2021. 433 in 2022, the number on her 2024 slide.
A year later, her slide said over a thousand.
To be exact: IBM's Condor chip, December 2023, held 1,121 qubits. The red pen fixes one digit.
Our physicist holds two. The student is still counting.
One honest catch: that 1,121-qubit chip was a research test.
The machines people run code on today have about 100 to 160 qubits, as of October 2026.
More qubits only help if they make few mistakes. After the big chip, IBM put a smaller chip with fewer errors online.
And behind the door, there was no longer one kind of machine. There were five.
Superconducting circuits: metal loops on a chip that carry current with no resistance.
Ions held in a row in a vacuum.
Neutral atoms in a grid, chilled by lasers.
Photons, particles of light; their builders say light is easier to scale.
And silicon spins, where each qubit is almost a transistor, so it can be made in chip factories.
Five kinds, no winner yet. The student can't pick a stall.
Which raises a question: does every quantum computer live in a freezer?
The superconducting ones do: about a hundredth of a degree above absolute zero, over 100 times colder than deep space.
The metal only superconducts when it is cold. Hence the parka. And the others?
Ions and atoms float in a vacuum, chilled by lasers. The box can stay at room temperature, but some machines cool it anyway for a cleaner vacuum.
And light doesn't mind the heat, but the detectors that count single photons are kept very cold.
Her slide ends with one more arrow: the future six years, to a million qubits.
Company roadmaps do aim at about a million. Plans, not machines: one plans 2 million by 2030; others give no date.
So here is what changed: real machines, many kinds, all online.
Now they need people who write and compile programs for them.
That's why the physicist is holding the door open, and the student walks in, laptop under one arm.
Next time: what the field has already done.
